Jumping Kids

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Ntando Mahlangu, standing high on the podium at 2020 Paralympics with his two gold medals.
- Born with fibular hemimelia, a severe congenital condition that affects both legs from the knee down, Ntando spent the first decade of his life in a wheelchair.

16 year-old, Puseletso Mabote performing above expectations, setting a new African record going through to the finals.
- In 2010, at the age of five, Puseletso underwent an emergency amputation after a truck crashed into the vehicle transporting him to school.

Blade sprinter Tebogo Mofoking showing good progress with another African record.
Aged one, Tebogo had both legs amputated below the knee due to severe burns after coming into contact with boiling water.

All of them an inspiration to disabled people across South Africa and an example of what is possible for amputees with access to prosthetics and holistic rehabilitative support.

With an estimated 20 000 new amputees in South Africa every year, the back story on how they got there is down to the alchemy of two men - Johan Snyders and Michael Stevens - both with their own stories.


Further information:
When Michael Stevens was 12, he lost both his legs in a freak accident that almost claimed his life. It was 1992, his dad Geoff, a yachtsman, was overseas competing in the Barcelona Olympics. Michael, his older sister ( 22 years) and brother ( 19 years) went up to the Vaal Dam for a day where his parents owned a small cottage. Eskom had recently installed new power lines in the cottages on the plot. The weather a bit windy to sail, Michael found a land yacht (basically a wind surfer on wheels) climbed aboard and headed out towards the water, around the back of the cottages. Eskom had left behind some power lines which were too low (no warning signs anywhere ) and the yacht mast touched a high tension electricity wire. Michael was hit with 33 000 volts of electricity. Transformer in Vereeeniging

His brother Richard found him lying on the grass, which had caught alight from the heat of Michaels’s body. Richard tried to perform CPR and realised Michael had swallowed his tongue. He was rushed to Vereeniging Hospital, whose power had blown from Michael’s accident. Loaded into the ambulance they took him to Baragwaneth which in ‘92 had one of the best burn units in the country. In the ambulance he flatlined, was resuscitated, rushed into surgery at Bara where he flatlined again. The medical team waited 4 days just not sure if he would survive and then they recommended that both Michael’s legs be amputated as the risk of infection was too great. 70 % of his body was suffering from 3rd degree burns.

Michael: “My first memory is waking up that evening after the amputations. The next morning my family was there and told me I had been in an accident and that they had to amputate my legs. I spent the next seven months in Bara’s Burns Unit. I had burns to 70 percent of my body and underwent countless skin grafts, having at least 50 operations. I was moved to various other hospitals over the next year and a half, undergoing extensive plastic surgeries and physiotherapy sessions. During this, I went back to my old school, K.E.P.S, and had to repeat grade seven. My classmates prior to my accident raised money and bought me a wheelchair. I got my first set of quality prosthetics when I was 15. I never hid the fact that I didn’t have legs but I didn’t promote the fact either. I couldn’t play cricket, but I would always be on the field supporting the team. I also enrolled in rowing and soon realised I was pretty good at that.”

The family sued Eskom, but it was a case of David and Goliath, with Eskom delaying court dates and decisions. Michael’s father’s business collapsed in the time, his mother went out to work to support the family. When Michael was 15, Eskom offered a settlement and they took it. It paid for Michael’s education and prosthetics.

After matric, Michael backpacked around Europe for a year before studying at RAU and Wits. He eventually got into buying and selling property. “I was doing well when the market crashed and the banks cut my financing. I was forced to sell everything to pay off my properties. I desperately needed new sockets for my prosthetics at the time, but didn’t have two cents to rub together. At the time I was training to try and qualify for the London Paralympics for rowing and I’d heard about a man named Johan Snyders who manufactures prosthetics. I went for a consultation and we became friends”.

Johan Snyders, one of best prosthetists in the world, was brought up in Bronkelspruit. He decided on this profession after breaking his leg as a young boy. Johan studied at TUT (Tshwane University of Technology), and then did his apprenticeship (2006 – 2009) at a global leader in orthopaedics OSSUR, which is based in Iceland. They were developing prosthetics and socket technology for non-profit organisations in the third world. The moulds traditionally took weeks to make and then fit, with Johan the turn-around time was reduced to a day. Johan spent time while with OSSUR in Afghanistan, Pakistan and Palestine where he fitted amputees in record time in the deserts and mountain villages using battery-operated tools. He brought this expertise back to South Africa and started IceExpress, with vison to do this work for people who couldn’t necessarily afford these prosthetics.

Michael and Johan are a match made in heaven. Johan wanted to make a difference, Michael was stumbling around questioning his role in life ‘How does a kid coming from a disadvantaged background born into disability and poverty escape?’

They meet Ntando at a clinic, a big chubby kid in a wheel chair. He is their first recruit to Jumping Kids, a not-for-profit NGO.

Up to this period Michael only knew a handful of disabled people. His way of dealing with his own disability was to push himself to be ‘normal’. Suddenly he finds himself diving into the world of disability, dealing with issues and challenges he had never thought about.

Ntando is not only fitted with his first set of prosthetic blades by Jumping Kids, but taught to walk, given an education and a future in athletics. Their first case study.

At Jumping Kids the youngest child is a year old and the oldest is 18.

To date 170 kids have been impacted by Jumping Kids, not everyone is the success story of Ntando, Puseletso or Tebogo but they have already committed to entering more athletes for Paris Para.

The biggest challenge facing amputees is the financial cost of a prosthetic limb. Michael believes once this is overcome anything physical is possible. ‘I was lucky to have had a family that could afford to buy me prosthetic limbs, but there are hundreds of kids in South Africa who aren’t as lucky. Although prosthetic limbs can be made in an hour, the cost is frightening. A lot of children are referred to Jumping Kids by their doctor or hospital. Sometimes the doctor will ask us to be involved before the amputation and explain what’s required to get the best possible stump for the socket. In other instances, people call in and tell us about a child who needs our help.’

At Jumping Kids the dream is to not only provide affordable prosthetic solutions for the best results but also access to better education and sport which can translate into the children’s long term reintegration as valuable members of society. A holistic approach.

This work is a calling and costs are not always met. Michael and Johan might be committed but they are at the end of their own road, funding a lot of the costs themselves.

Script:


V/O
Ntando Mahlangu, with his double gold at the Tokyo Paralympics ….
….16 year-old, Paralympian, Puseletso Mabote,
Blade sprinter, Tebogo Mofoking PAUSE a small sample of amputees around the country whose lives have been turned around due to the partnership of two men - Johan Snyders and Michael Stevens - both with their own histories.

Michael: My brother found me he said I was lying on the grass and that I had set the grass around me alight it was starting to smoulder. He came to do CPR, he opened my mouth I had swallowed my tongue, he brought my tongue out I started to scream, he knew I was alive.

Link: When Michael Stevens was 12, he lost both his legs in a freak accident that almost claimed his life. It was 1992 Michael, his 22 year old brother Richard and 25 year old sister Carolynn decided to spend the day at the Vaal Dam.

Carollyn: It was a perfect day. I, my middle brother Richard and Michael and we all just got into the car, It was a very normal thing we had done often.

Michael: So the weather wasn’t great for sailing there was a land yacht which is essentially a wind surfer with wheels, put a sail on it and you can go on sand roads and let the wind drive you. So we set that up I jumped on first.

Link: Eskom had recently installed new power lines for the cottages at the club… They were laid too low with no Safety or Warning signs. As Michael land sped towards the dam his mast touched a high tension electricity wire.

Link: Michael was hit with 33 000 volts of electricity

Carollyn: Richard and I at the same time said where is Michael and it was if the world went dead quiet, GAP we could just see smoke he was on fire his clothes were burning, I picked Michael up and his back was just jelly it was terrible I could see all the way through his ankle to his bone, his shoes had melted.

V/O
Michael landed up at Chris Hani Baragwaneth Hospital, which in 1992 had one of the best burn units in the country.

Link : The medical team waited 3 days to see Michael would survive and then recommended that both his legs be amputated as the risk of infection was too high. 70 % of his body was suffering from 3rd degree burns.

Gaynor It was that or he’d die, the legs were dead.

Michael: What they said to my mom is once you survive your electrocution …the biggest risk to my life was infection because I essentially had no skin left on my body, I had my face my chest and my stomach.

Gaynor: He was obviously very drugged and he just looked at me and said no I am going to live don’t worry mom and then he was in and out of consciousness.

V/O
After seven months at Chris Hani Baragwaneth, Michael spent the next year undergoing skin grafts, and more procedures.

Gaynor: The first time they allowed him to come home he weighed 19 kilograms, thin waif bandages everywhere.

Link: It was advised he go to a school for the disabled but Michael was adamant he wanted return to King Edwards Preparatory School,/

Michael: in a wheel chair bandaged head to toe…no toes. I had people pushing my chair and jumping me over things not really thinking about it just having fun with me which was scary and great.

Link: His ambitions to play cricket for the country might not be achievable but he was soon part of the rowing team, despite no legs

Gaynor: He used to leave his legs on the side get in. Once Mike was mobile Mike was mobile.

Claire: Lets ff now and talk about meeting Johan Snyders, how did that happen?
Michael: I was trying to make the SA Paralympics for Rowing and one day at one of the training sessions Johan arrived he was telling me about this non profit he had started for disabled kids. I could tell we were on the same wave length.

V/O
Johan had interned and worked at OSSUR in Iceland - a company world renowned for its work in orthopaedics – Johan became part of the team revolutionising the making and fitting of prosthetics for developing countries.

Johan: In general prosthetics are a lengthy process in the current government hospitals, it’s a 4 to 6 week’s delivery period to make and actual prosthesis. So if you are from a rural area you have to travel in and out to go for prosthetic fitting. Its costly and if it doesn’t fit you have to travel all the way back, . So we would see the amputees, we would manufacture a prosthesis, you would assemble it on the same session and then you could start rehabilitation immediately.

V/O
With OSSUR Johan travelled to Angola, Mozambique, , to deserts and hard to get to villages, fitting amputees with their innovative prosthetics, that could be manufactured and fitted in one session.

We made some difference earthquake in Pakistan and the disasters in Haiti and I had a stint in Gaza so its nice to work in some of these countries and then transfer technology get the local guys involved and teach them how to do this and then they can be independent when you leave.

Link: Michael Stevens and Johan Snyders, a perfect partnership Johan wanted to make a difference, Michael was questioning his role in life ‘How does a kid coming from a disadvantaged background born into disability and poverty escape?’

V/O
And Jumping Kids, was the result …Ntando Mchlangu was one of their first beneficiaries. In 2012 he was fitted with a set prosthetic blades by Johan.

Ntando: I went to see Johan in this room he was sitting there I was sitting here and he asked me and he said young man how can I help you and I said to him I just want to run and I think me and him the connection between me and him it started then.

Johan: We fitted him with a pair of blades and he took to it like a duck to water

Ntando: Johan was keeping contact with the school and he was asking how is Ntando doing and they told him Ntando is walking without his crutches, what how within a period of 5 days so ja its been a beautiful journey.

V/O
It could have been a very different journey. Michaels first legs came care of a state hospital.

Michael: I look at this and I wonder how you move.
Claire: What a contraption
Michael; Correct, and in theory it’s about safety but what they have done is make it unusable. I wore it for about a year and this is where I gave up and went back into the wheelchair. Kids like Ntando the double above the knew amputees, they get its just one piece down to the bottom with a round circle, rubber pad to the bottom and they are done cheers go…and they are heavy, heavy that’s what they are given to walk

V/O
Jumping Kids get Ntando into a mainstream school, which unlike the disabled school offers matric and sport. He is their first case study, a blue print of a holistic rehabilitation of an amputee.

Michael: The moment we got him into schools and started to get things going. We knew it was the trajectory that he could make Rio.

V/O
Ntando’s silver at Rio Paralympics was just a prelude of what was to come

Ntando : I am at a place now where its my job is to inspire and create opportunities for others, giving children of South Africa an opportunity to be mobile and to move around.

V/O
Ntando is already paying it forward.

Puseletso Mabote came into the Jumping Kids stable when he was 7 years. He had an emergency amputation after a car crash when he was five.

Puseletso: When I saw the Paralympics for the first time. I was inspired my Ntando, I saw his 200 m race and I was Ya I want to be like that. And then ff a year I went to my first international competition that’s where Johan saw that I have potential,

V/O
Five years later in 2019 Puseletso started at King Edward High School, that same year he set a new world record in the men’s 200 m at World Para Athletics Junior Championships and then there was the 2020 Tokyo Paralympics

Puseletso: I have already achieved my first goal for Para just getting there make finals now I want to achieve that world record and get gold in the next Para so I am really aiming for Paris 2024

V/O
At Jumping Kids the youngest child is a year old and the oldest 18, and while not everyone is an athlete, they have the access to write their own story.

Michael: When I stepped into it naively again with an idea that aah you can do some good you have a year to figure out lets go do this but it was more than that it was a calling. Its evolved and its become something I can’t walk away from anymore.

Claire: You are changing peoples lives?
Michael I am also changing my own.

Michael: What they said to my mom is once you survive your electrocution …the biggest risk to my life was infection because I essentially had no skin left on my body, I had my face my chest and my stomach. Gaynor: He was obviously very drugged and he just looked at me and said no I am going to live don’t worry mom and then he was in and out of consciousness. V/O After seven months at Chris Hani Baragwaneth, Michael spent the next year undergoing skin grafts, and more procedures. Gaynor: The first time they allowed him to come home he weighed 19 kilograms, thin waif bandages everywhere. Link: It was advised he go to a school for the disabled but Michael was adamant he wanted return to King Edwards Preparatory School,/ Michael: in a wheel chair bandaged head to toe…no toes. I had people pushing my chair and jumping me over things not really thinking about it just having fun with me which was scary and great. Link: His ambitions to play cricket for the country might not be achievable but he was soon part of the rowing team, despite no legs Gaynor: He used to leave his legs on the side get in. Once Mike was mobile Mike was mobile. Claire: Lets ff now and talk about meeting Johan Snyders, how did that happen? Michael: I was trying to make the SA Paralympics for Rowing and one day at one of the training sessions Johan arrived he was telling me about this non profit he had started for disabled kids. I could tell we were on the same wave length. V/O Johan had interned and worked at OSSUR in Iceland - a company world renowned for its work in orthopaedics – Johan became part of the team revolutionising the making and fitting of prosthetics for developing countries. Johan: In general prosthetics are a lengthy process in the current government hospitals, it’s a 4 to 6 week’s delivery period to make and actual prosthesis. So if you are from a rural area you have to travel in and out to go for prosthetic fitting. Its costly and if it doesn’t fit you have to travel all the way back, . So we would see the amputees, we would manufacture a prosthesis, you would assemble it on the same session and then you could start rehabilitation immediately. V/O With OSSUR Johan travelled to Angola, Mozambique, , to deserts and hard to get to villages, fitting amputees with their innovative prosthetics, that could be manufactured and fitted in one session. We made some difference earthquake in Pakistan and the disasters in Haiti and I had a stint in Gaza so its nice to work in some of these countries and then transfer technology get the local guys involved and teach them how to do this and then they can be independent when you leave. Link: Michael Stevens and Johan Snyders, a perfect partnership Johan wanted to make a difference, Michael was questioning his role in life ‘How does a kid coming from a disadvantaged background born into disability and poverty escape?’ V/O And Jumping Kids, was the result …Ntando Mchlangu was one of their first beneficiaries. In 2012 he was fitted with a set prosthetic blades by Johan. Ntando: I went to see Johan in this room he was sitting there I was sitting here and he asked me and he said young man how can I help you and I said to him I just want to run and I think me and him the connection between me and him it started then. Johan: We fitted him with a pair of blades and he took to it like a duck to water Ntando: Johan was keeping contact with the school and he was asking how is Ntando doing and they told him Ntando is walking without his crutches, what how within a period of 5 days so ja its been a beautiful journey. V/O It could have been a very different journey. Michaels first legs came care of a state hospital. Michael: I look at this and I wonder how you move. Claire: What a contraption Michael; Correct, and in theory it’s about safety but what they have done is make it unusable. I wore it for about a year and this is where I gave up and went back into the wheelchair. Kids like Ntando the double above the knew amputees, they get its just one piece down to the bottom with a round circle, rubber pad to the bottom and they are done cheers go…and they are heavy, heavy that’s what they are given to walk V/O Jumping Kids get Ntando into a mainstream school, which unlike the disabled school offers matric and sport. He is their first case study, a blue print of a holistic rehabilitation of an amputee. Michael: The moment we got him into schools and started to get things going. We knew it was the trajectory that he could make Rio. V/O Ntando’s silver at Rio Paralympics was just a prelude of what was to come Ntando : I am at a place now where its my job is to inspire and create opportunities for others, giving children of South Africa an opportunity to be mobile and to move around. V/O Ntando is already paying it forward. Puseletso Mabote came into the Jumping Kids stable when he was 7 years. He had an emergency amputation after a car crash when he was five. Puseletso: When I saw the Paralympics for the first time. I was inspired my Ntando, I saw his 200 m race and I was Ya I want to be like that. And then ff a year I went to my first international competition that’s where Johan saw that I have potential, V/O Five years later in 2019 Puseletso started at King Edward High School, that same year he set a new world record in the men’s 200 m at World Para Athletics Junior Championships and then there was the 2020 Tokyo Paralympics Puseletso: I have already achieved my first goal for Para just getting there make finals now I want to achieve that world record and get gold in the next Para so I am really aiming for Paris 2024 V/O At Jumping Kids the youngest child is a year old and the oldest 18, and while not everyone is an athlete, they have the access to write their own story. Michael: When I stepped into it naively again with an idea that aah you can do some good you have a year to figure out lets go do this but it was more than that it was a calling. Its evolved and its become something I can’t walk away from anymore. Claire: You are changing peoples lives? Michael I am also changing my own.

metadata.Summary: Ntando Mahlangu, standing high on the podium at 2020 Paralympics with his two gold medals. - Born with fibular hemimelia, a severe congenital condition that affects both legs from the knee down, Ntando spent the first decade of his life in a wheelchair. 16 year-old, Puseletso Mabote performing above expectations, setting a new African record going through to the finals. - In 2010, at the age of five, Puseletso underwent an emergency amputation after a truck crashed into the vehicle transporting him to school. Blade sprinter Tebogo Mofoking showing good progress with another African record. Aged one, Tebogo had both legs amputated below the knee due to severe burns after coming into contact with boiling water. All of them an inspiration to disabled people across South Africa and an example of what is possible for amputees with access to prosthetics and holistic rehabilitative support. With an estimated 20 000 new amputees in South Africa every year, the back story on how they got there is down to the alchemy of two men - Johan Snyders and Michael Stevens - both with their own stories.
metadata.Further information: When Michael Stevens was 12, he lost both his legs in a freak accident that almost claimed his life. It was 1992, his dad Geoff, a yachtsman, was overseas competing in the Barcelona Olympics. Michael, his older sister ( 22 years) and brother ( 19 years) went up to the Vaal Dam for a day where his parents owned a small cottage. Eskom had recently installed new power lines in the cottages on the plot. The weather a bit windy to sail, Michael found a land yacht (basically a wind surfer on wheels) climbed aboard and headed out towards the water, around the back of the cottages. Eskom had left behind some power lines which were too low (no warning signs anywhere ) and the yacht mast touched a high tension electricity wire. Michael was hit with 33 000 volts of electricity. Transformer in Vereeeniging His brother Richard found him lying on the grass, which had caught alight from the heat of Michaels’s body. Richard tried to perform CPR and realised Michael had swallowed his tongue. He was rushed to Vereeniging Hospital, whose power had blown from Michael’s accident. Loaded into the ambulance they took him to Baragwaneth which in ‘92 had one of the best burn units in the country. In the ambulance he flatlined, was resuscitated, rushed into surgery at Bara where he flatlined again. The medical team waited 4 days just not sure if he would survive and then they recommended that both Michael’s legs be amputated as the risk of infection was too great. 70 % of his body was suffering from 3rd degree burns. Michael: “My first memory is waking up that evening after the amputations. The next morning my family was there and told me I had been in an accident and that they had to amputate my legs. I spent the next seven months in Bara’s Burns Unit. I had burns to 70 percent of my body and underwent countless skin grafts, having at least 50 operations. I was moved to various other hospitals over the next year and a half, undergoing extensive plastic surgeries and physiotherapy sessions. During this, I went back to my old school, K.E.P.S, and had to repeat grade seven. My classmates prior to my accident raised money and bought me a wheelchair. I got my first set of quality prosthetics when I was 15. I never hid the fact that I didn’t have legs but I didn’t promote the fact either. I couldn’t play cricket, but I would always be on the field supporting the team. I also enrolled in rowing and soon realised I was pretty good at that.” The family sued Eskom, but it was a case of David and Goliath, with Eskom delaying court dates and decisions. Michael’s father’s business collapsed in the time, his mother went out to work to support the family. When Michael was 15, Eskom offered a settlement and they took it. It paid for Michael’s education and prosthetics. After matric, Michael backpacked around Europe for a year before studying at RAU and Wits. He eventually got into buying and selling property. “I was doing well when the market crashed and the banks cut my financing. I was forced to sell everything to pay off my properties. I desperately needed new sockets for my prosthetics at the time, but didn’t have two cents to rub together. At the time I was training to try and qualify for the London Paralympics for rowing and I’d heard about a man named Johan Snyders who manufactures prosthetics. I went for a consultation and we became friends”. Johan Snyders, one of best prosthetists in the world, was brought up in Bronkelspruit. He decided on this profession after breaking his leg as a young boy. Johan studied at TUT (Tshwane University of Technology), and then did his apprenticeship (2006 – 2009) at a global leader in orthopaedics OSSUR, which is based in Iceland. They were developing prosthetics and socket technology for non-profit organisations in the third world. The moulds traditionally took weeks to make and then fit, with Johan the turn-around time was reduced to a day. Johan spent time while with OSSUR in Afghanistan, Pakistan and Palestine where he fitted amputees in record time in the deserts and mountain villages using battery-operated tools. He brought this expertise back to South Africa and started IceExpress, with vison to do this work for people who couldn’t necessarily afford these prosthetics. Michael and Johan are a match made in heaven. Johan wanted to make a difference, Michael was stumbling around questioning his role in life ‘How does a kid coming from a disadvantaged background born into disability and poverty escape?’ They meet Ntando at a clinic, a big chubby kid in a wheel chair. He is their first recruit to Jumping Kids, a not-for-profit NGO. Up to this period Michael only knew a handful of disabled people. His way of dealing with his own disability was to push himself to be ‘normal’. Suddenly he finds himself diving into the world of disability, dealing with issues and challenges he had never thought about. Ntando is not only fitted with his first set of prosthetic blades by Jumping Kids, but taught to walk, given an education and a future in athletics. Their first case study. At Jumping Kids the youngest child is a year old and the oldest is 18. To date 170 kids have been impacted by Jumping Kids, not everyone is the success story of Ntando, Puseletso or Tebogo but they have already committed to entering more athletes for Paris Para. The biggest challenge facing amputees is the financial cost of a prosthetic limb. Michael believes once this is overcome anything physical is possible. ‘I was lucky to have had a family that could afford to buy me prosthetic limbs, but there are hundreds of kids in South Africa who aren’t as lucky. Although prosthetic limbs can be made in an hour, the cost is frightening. A lot of children are referred to Jumping Kids by their doctor or hospital. Sometimes the doctor will ask us to be involved before the amputation and explain what’s required to get the best possible stump for the socket. In other instances, people call in and tell us about a child who needs our help.’ At Jumping Kids the dream is to not only provide affordable prosthetic solutions for the best results but also access to better education and sport which can translate into the children’s long term reintegration as valuable members of society. A holistic approach. This work is a calling and costs are not always met. Michael and Johan might be committed but they are at the end of their own road, funding a lot of the costs themselves.
